### Two threads
• Two threads fit in the window at once. ⌥⌘1 to 9 puts that thread of the drawer beside the open one, and so do ⌥-click on its row, Open Beside in the row's menu and in the Thread menu, and ⌘K's Open beside…. Each has its own message bar, with its own model button, queue and Stop, so you can write to both and both can work at the same time. The keyboard is in one of them: a click anywhere in a column puts you there, ⌥⌘← and ⌥⌘→ do it from the keys, and the title, the review and ⌘K follow it. ⌥⌘W, Close Other Side, or the cross on the other thread's title puts that side away and stops nothing. There is never a third, and ⌘N with two in view gives the new thread the whole window until its first message, after which the one beside is back. Where the window hasn't about 440 points for each, the pair folds to the thread you're writing in, either arrow shows the other, and a thread asked for beside says "Widen the window to see both". Quit, and the same two come back on the same sides. The arrows and ⌥⌘W can be given other keys in Settings › Shortcuts; if one of them, or ⌥⌘ with a digit, was already a key of yours for something else, it stays yours. • What you type stays with its thread. Open another thread and the field shows that one's own draft; come back and yours is there, with its pictures and its `$` prompt. The text of a draft outlasts a quit, in every thread that has had its first message. Its pictures, its queue and a `$` prompt don't, and neither does text in a thread you never sent anything to. • In a pair the model button gives up its level's word and then its model's name as its column narrows, so the field keeps its room. The keyboard is in the message bar when the app opens.
### Witness, the review
• Witness is the review now, and ⌘⇧D opens it. It starts with one sentence about the checks, "make test last ran before RootView.swift last changed. It was piped through tail, so its result is not known.", then Read first, the changes to read before any other, each with its reason in words: changed after a check last ran, words taken out of a line, changes what a test expects, deleted. Under that each check's last run has a row saying exited 0, failed, or result not known and why, then the rest in the order the thread touched the files, then Spacing, moves and lockfiles, a line each. No model is called for any of it, and nothing on the page says a check passed. The review as it was is one setting away: Settings › Source control › Review, Legacy. • In Witness a change reads as code. One column of numbers, a green edge beside an added line, the old line in red above a replaced one with the words that went washed, and a removal of more than six lines as one row that → opens. J and K walk by change, Space marks a change reviewed and goes to the next, as a click in the number column marks it, ⇧Space marks the file, N leaves a note, ⌫ takes a change back, O opens the file at its line. T shows the edit in the thread, lit for a moment, and A writes a note asking for the check again, unpiped, which goes only when you send it. What can be done to a change is also in a right-click on it and in the header's "…". → on a run's row shows the last twelve lines it printed. Under the page a caption says of the change the keyboard is on which message asked for it, how often its file was edited and with which runs between, and what the agent said before the edit. The commit button says what it takes, "Commit 9 Files" or "Commit 4 Reviewed". Code in Witness has no syntax colours and can't be selected; the change's menu has Copy. • Three keys do something else than they did. Tab and ⇧Tab walk by file, and reach the commit message only past the last one, where Tab used to go straight to it. ← and → open and close a long removal where they folded a file. O opens the file at the change's line, not at its top. • Witness knows more runs than the main agent's own. A command you run at the shell prompt counts as a check, so does one a Claude Code subagent ran, and one sent to the background says how it ended once it has. Settings › Source control › This project's check names a command of your project's own, ./ci.sh say, to be read as make test is. A result is known where the agent's word is the command's own ending, which is Claude Code, Codex and your shell prompt, or where the call carries an exit code, looked for in Cursor's and OpenCode's. Pi, Antigravity and Command Code send none, and none has been seen from Copilot, Grok Build or Devin, so a run of theirs stays "result not known". So does any run with something after the check other than &&: a pipe, a `;`, an `||`. • What Witness doesn't see. Only checks run since the last commit are on the page. Agents pipe most test runs through something, so expect "result not known" on most rows until a check is run bare, which is what A asks for. A thread brought in from a Terminal session has no times, so all of it is Read first until a check runs in OriCode. A subagent given a worktree of its own isn't read. • An edit in the transcript is drawn as the review draws it: its first twelve lines open, with their numbers, the green edge and the old line in red, and a line at the foot counting the rest. A click on the card's header opens the review on that file's change; the path in it no longer opens the file, which O in the review does. The card doesn't fold any more, so a thread of many edits is a good deal taller than it was. A line longer than the card is cut at its edge and whole in the review. With Legacy chosen the card is the folded one it was, its path a link.
### Threads that open and read each other
• Ask a thread for another, "open another thread and have it fix that in the other repo", and it opens one. It is an ordinary thread, in the drawer from its first message, on the agent, model and permissions of the one that opened it unless you named others, in the same folder, in another project you've added, or on a branch of its own. The first thread carries on, and when the other's first turn ends it gets one line, "… finished its first turn" or "… stopped before its first turn finished", which a click opens beside. A thread opened this way can't open another, and one turn opens three at most. This and the two below need an agent that takes OriCode's tools, which Pi, Command Code, Antigravity and Grok Build don't. • A thread can suggest one too. When the agent comes across something outside what you asked, a bug in passing or a test that was already failing, a button with its title sits under the reply; a click opens a new thread in the same project with the prompt written in the message bar, unsent. Nothing starts until you send it, and a turn offers two at most. So far it has been seen from Claude Code only, and not from every model: Sonnet and Opus offered one unasked where Haiku didn't. • Threads can read each other. Ask one "which thread changed Drawer.swift?" and it lists the project's threads with the files each edited, and it can read another's transcript, the one it opened included. An edit here is one an agent made with its edit tool; a file changed by a shell command, sed or a script, has no thread to its name, and the answer says so. Reading is all it can do to a thread that exists: it can't message, steer or stop one.
### Smaller
• The drawer's project menu has No folder, after your projects, so a thread tied to no project is one pick away from inside any of them. ⌘K's Reveal in Finder is Open project folder in Finder, which opens the folder the thread works in, its worktree for a thread on its own branch, and answers to "open", "folder" and "path" as well as "reveal". • A thread that came up as empty glass, its title and its message bar there and no messages until you sent one, now finds its own end. • J or K pressed in the first moment of the review opening no longer quits the app. In Legacy, a file opened after the page was made shows its changes. • Words no longer run into each other, or get squeezed to dots, in a narrow window. The review's header stays on one line, its branch and file name giving way in the middle; the commit message takes a row of its own over the buttons when there's no room beside them; a pinned drawer stands aside while the review is up in a window too narrow for both; an open file ends above a tall message bar; and what git said of a refused push runs on as one line under the composer, as far as the line has room, and whole under the pointer. • A streaming reply does about an eighth less work for each piece of text that arrives, and ⌘K's search does less for each letter. For the first, the paragraph still being written can't be selected, and a link in it doesn't click, until it ends or half a second passes with no new word.
